title: Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co.
lead: A Hawaiian paving contractor commits to fixed-price jobs under a long-term asphalt relationship, then faces a sharp price increase without the protection Shell had provided on the only two earlier increases.

actors.name: Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co.
actors.role: Grace Brothers division and Hawaii’s second-largest asphaltic paving contractor; Shell’s requirements buyer.

actors.name: Shell Oil Co.
actors.role: Asphalt supplier seeking greater Hawaiian volume through its long-term relationship with Nanakuli.

actors.name: Bohner
actors.role: Shell’s local representative, familiar with Nanakuli’s bids, projects, and material requirements.

actors.name: Chevron and Hawaiian Bitumuls
actors.role: The other principal asphalt supplier and Nanakuli’s principal paving competitor; their relationship supplied comparison evidence.

proceedings: Nanakuli sued in Hawaii state court in February 1976; Shell removed the case on March 2.
The jury awarded $220,800 for denied price protection but rejected two other claims; the district court set aside the award.
The Ninth Circuit reinstated the verdict with lawful interest and remanded for final judgment on December 21, 1981.
limits: The panel reviewed evidence in the verdict winner’s favor rather than independently resolving credibility. The rejected commissions and shortage-profit claims did not become awards. Later protections under other contracts were not additional performance episodes under the 1969 contract. The account concerns the historical Hawaii Code.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: The contractor and supplier build a mutually dependent relationship
sections.cue: Why did local bidding practices matter to their arrangement?
paragraphs: Nanakuli, a division of Grace Brothers and Hawaii's second-largest asphaltic paving contractor, began with smaller paving jobs on Oahu and sought larger government contracts against Hawaiian Bitumuls, whose asphalt came from Chevron. Shell needed greater volume to expand in Hawaii, while Nanakuli needed dependable supply and competitive prices. Shell built a terminal and supplied Nanakuli’s asphalt requirements from 1963 through 1974 under successive long-term arrangements. A distributorship commission largely operated as a discount because Nanakuli consumed most of the asphalt itself. Witnesses described the closeness as a partnership, and Nanakuli displayed Shell colors and its logo, but the court did not establish a legal partnership.

When Nanakuli’s quarry landlord demanded improved facilities, Nanakuli estimated $250,000–$300,000 in investment. Shell considered financing but instead offered a further volume discount and joined meetings with Nanakuli’s bank. On April 1, 1969, the parties executed supply, distributorship, and discount arrangements tied to loan amortization. They ran through December 31, 1975, with cancellation thereafter on six months’ notice, producing a minimum term exceeding seven years. The writing set the asphalt price at Shell’s posted price on delivery, free on board Honolulu.

Major government paving jobs generally barred material-price escalation, and general contractors usually refused to pass increases through. A paver could bid, receive a later award, and remain locked into a price despite rising material costs. “Price protection” meant holding the old price temporarily or for quantities committed to such work, commonly with advance notice of increases. Nanakuli would contend that this commercial practice formed part of its written bargain.

sources.pinpoint: 664 F.2d at 777–784 & n.4; A mutually dependent supply relationship

sections.title: Shell protects earlier work but its later management refuses
paragraphs: Under the 1969 agreement, Shell protected Nanakuli through the only two pre-1974 price increases: four months in 1970 and three months in 1971. Manager Blee, who knew the negotiated arrangement, discussed in an internal memorandum how long existing work should be protected, rather than simply denying any obligation.

A November 1970 general policy letter asked for a new firm commitment within fifteen days of a project award. A similar letter followed in November 1973. Their significance was disputed: the earlier letter promised to honor existing commitments, and the later letter arrived after the relevant projects had been bid, according to Nanakuli. Bohner, Shell’s local representative, frequently visited, followed winning bids, sometimes attended openings, and knew supply needs before shipments from California. That familiarity helped explain why Nanakuli did not repeatedly send formal project notices.

Shell then raised its price from $44 to $76 per ton effective January 1, 1974. A letter dated December 31 reached Nanakuli on January 4. The oil embargo tightened supply and raised petroleum costs, although asphalt itself was not subject to federal petroleum price controls. Nanakuli requested protection for 7,200 tons already committed at the old price, wrote repeatedly, and met Shell’s new mainland managers.

Those managers replaced officials involved in the 1969 negotiations. At the meeting, they had not previously seen the three contracts and knew nothing of the earlier protection. They searched incomplete files rather than effectively consulting the local representative. They denied protection based on the delivery-price term and current company policy.

sources.pinpoint: 664 F.2d at 785–789, 805 & nn.18, 20–25; Performance; Shell’s notices

sections.title: A jury accepts one claim and the trial judge sets it aside
paragraphs: Nanakuli sued in Hawaii state court in February 1976, and Shell removed the action on March 2. The jury awarded $220,800 for denied price protection. It rejected claims for commissions and discounts on substitute asphalt bought elsewhere and profits lost when shortages forced abandonment of signed work. The district court entered judgment notwithstanding the verdict on the favorable claim.

Nanakuli appealed, and Shell cross-appealed evidentiary rulings. The Ninth Circuit had to consider all evidence and reasonable inferences in Nanakuli’s favor without weighing credibility, asking whether reasonable jurors could find breach. The panel was not making fresh factual findings.

Nanakuli advanced two routes: local trade usage, reinforced by performance, supplied a price-protection term; alternatively, commercial good faith governed implementation of the increase. Shell disputed the relevant trade’s breadth, called earlier protection gratuitous waivers, argued that usage contradicted the express price term, and challenged the practice’s precision for damages.

sections.title: Local evidence supports a usage broader than identical-product sellers
sections.cue: Why could the jury consider aggregate suppliers but not cement suppliers?
paragraphs: Hawaii's Uniform Commercial Code recognized regular observance in a place, vocation, or trade sufficient to justify expected compliance, including practices parties knew or should have known. A seller’s obligations were not necessarily limited to customs of sellers of its identical product. The panel allowed asphalt and aggregate evidence from Hawaii’s asphaltic-paving trade because of the small market, two principal asphalt suppliers, Shell’s investment in Nanakuli’s growth, and Bohner’s close knowledge of bidding and materials. Cement played too small and infrequent a role, so its exclusion was upheld.

Bohner’s construction involvement and familiarity with aggregate allowed jurors to infer more knowledge than his cautious trial testimony acknowledged. This conclusion rested on the unusually close relationship and market, not a rule charging every seller with all buyer-side customs.

Two experienced aggregate suppliers described a practice predating 1969: pavers supplied lists of committed jobs or tonnage, and suppliers trusted them without demanding separate written orders. Documents corroborated that account. Chevron routinely protected Hawaiian Bitumuls, including 12,000 tons in March 1969, despite silence in their writing. Chevron’s earlier ownership connection affected weight, not automatic admissibility. Shell identified no Hawaiian paving supplier that refused comparable protection before its own 1974 refusal.

The Code did not require immemorial or universal custom; sufficiently regular observance creating justified expectations sufficed. Here the evidence supported a dominant, effectively universal local pattern. Existence and scope were ordinarily factual questions, apart from interpretation of a written trade code.

sections.title: Performance and the posted price can describe one bounded bargain
sections.cue: Why did the express term not conclusively defeat the verdict?
paragraphs: A single act did not establish a course of performance under the cited comment, but no mechanical minimum barred treating the two occasions calling for protection as performance of an understood duty. The preference for construing ambiguous conduct as waiver preserved flexibility and avoided surprise or hardship; jurors could find these episodes clear enough to show agreement instead. Later protection generally identified as occurring in 1977 and 1978 involved different contracts, with some uncertainty in witness year references. Those episodes were not additional performance under the 1969 agreement.

The Code’s factual agreement included commercial context. Performance, dealing before the agreement, and trade usage served different roles. Express terms prevailed if reasonable reconciliation failed, followed by performance, dealing, and usage, but contextual evidence did not require facial ambiguity or an incomplete writing. The court surveyed price, quantity, and delivery decisions while insisting that a practice be established, sufficiently specific, and suitable to comparable transactions, with an objective basis preventing post-dispute rewriting.

This protection did not transfer price-setting power to Nanakuli. It held old prices temporarily or for committed work at an increase; Shell’s posted price governed the remaining purchases. The jury could reconcile that bounded exception with the writing. The comparable long-term Chevron arrangement supported that conclusion.

The 1970 letter did not conclusively extinguish the bargain. Award-stage commitments left bid-to-award increases exposed, Shell could not unilaterally terminate an existing contractual protection, and Nanakuli could regard its long-term agreement as a prior commitment the letter honored. The letter also referred to purchase-date pricing rather than the agreement’s delivery-date price. Courteous requests for protection did not concede the absence of legal entitlement.

sections.title: The jury had an adequate basis for damages and an alternative good-faith theory
sections.cue: What was wrong with how the price increase was implemented?
paragraphs: Differences in protection by time or tonnage did not make damages impermissibly uncertain. Code remedies sought the performance position with the precision the evidence allowed. Shell’s earlier protected quantities and Chevron’s 12,000-ton protection supplied concrete references, while Nanakuli’s growth explained the larger 1974 commitment. The panel upheld the jury’s $220,800 figure; it did not identify that award as the simple unadjusted product of 7,200 tons and the $32 increase.

The alternative theory invoked good faith in a seller-set price and merchants’ reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing. A posted price normally met the standard, but the challenge concerned implementation, not the $76 amount. Shell gave no advance notice and refused protection for committed jobs. Chevron charged the same new price but gave at least six weeks’ notice. That directly comparable asphalt evidence supported the verdict even though aggregate suppliers did not share petroleum-specific constraints.

The panel did not announce that every later usage proved an expectation when contracting. Later asphalt evidence was relevant to 1974 fair dealing; limited later aggregate evidence caused no prejudice. Similarly, the court criticized treating boilerplate merger and waiver clauses as a blanket exclusion of commercial context, but did not need to decide whether refusal of further deposition excerpts was an abuse of discretion. The sufficient admitted record supported reinstatement without a new trial on all excluded material.

sections.title: Kennedy insists on objective commercial standards and the verdict is restored
sections.cue: What exact relief did Nanakuli obtain?
paragraphs: Judge Kennedy concurred specially. A specific protection obligation could not arise from generalized unfairness alone; established custom, usage, or other objective standards known clearly to the parties were necessary. The largely uncontradicted local evidence permitted a finding that both firms knew or should have known the practice when contracting. Kennedy regarded that foundation as necessary under either the implied-term or good-faith route.

Senior District Judge Hoffman, sitting by designation with Chief Judge Browning and Kennedy, wrote the principal opinion. On December 21, 1981, the unanimous panel reversed the judgment, reinstated the $220,800 price-protection verdict with interest according to law, and remanded with directions to enter final judgment. It did not merely reopen factfinding, and the two rejected claims remained rejected. Rehearing was denied February 8, 1982.

sources.pinpoint: 664 F.2d at 777, 806; Exact judgment and complete source
